subtract-from-a-date.quickAnswer: Going backwards is calendar arithmetic in reverse: move back from the start date by the chosen days, weeks, months or years. For example, 90 days before 18 October 2026 is 20 July 2026, a Monday. Month subtraction keeps the same day number where possible - 1 month before 31 March lands on 3 March (2 March in a leap year), because February has no 31st.
keyFacts: Subtracting days is exact: the calendar moves back one day at a time, so 90 days before 18 October 2026 is 20 July 2026.
Subtracting months keeps the same day number when the target month has that day. 1 month before 31 May is 30 April, because April has only 30 days.
Subtracting years keeps the same month and day. 1 year before 29 February 2024 is 28 February 2023.
Weeks are exact groups of 7 days, so subtracting weeks never changes the weekday: 3 weeks before a Monday is always a Monday.
Leap years are handled automatically in reverse too.
howTo: Pick your start date using the date picker.
Enter how much time you want to subtract, as a whole number.
Choose the unit: days, weeks, months or years.
Read the resulting past date, its weekday and its ISO (YYYY-MM-DD) form instantly.
Use the days-ago figure to see how far in the past the result lies.
subtract-from-a-date.formula:
Result = start date - N units.
Days: result = start date - N days.
Weeks: result = start date - (N x 7) days.
Months: result month = start month - N (day kept when valid).
Years: result year = start year - N (same month and day).
Example: 2026-10-18 - 90 days = 2026-07-20.
subtract-from-a-date.workedExample:
Start date: 18 October 2026 (a Sunday). Amount: 90, unit: days.
1. October: 18 - 17 = 1 October (17 days used).
2. September: 30 more days -> 1 September (47 used).
3. August: 31 more days -> 1 August (78 used).
4. July: 12 more days -> 20 July 2026 (90 used).
5. Weekday: 90 = 12 weeks + 6 days back, so Sunday - 6 = Monday.
Result: 20 July 2026, Monday. ISO: 2026-07-20.
benefits: Find past deadlines, anniversaries and historical dates in one click.
Month-end and leap-year edge cases handled automatically in reverse.
The weekday is shown with every result - great for 'what day was...' questions.
Runs fully in your browser - no account, no tracking, works offline.
limitations: Month arithmetic follows standard calendar rollover; legal or contract definitions of 'a month ago' may differ.
Public holidays and business days are not considered - this is pure calendar math.
Time zones are ignored - the output is a calendar date, not a timestamp.
Extremely large subtractions can exceed calendar support.

faqs.q: What happens when I subtract 1 month from 31 March?
faqs.a: You land on 3 March in non-leap years (2 March in leap years). The calendar rolls the invalid 31 February back into March - the mirror image of adding a month to 31 January.

faqs.q: Does subtracting weeks change the weekday?
faqs.a: Never. A week is exactly 7 days in either direction, so 6 weeks before a Wednesday is always a Wednesday.

faqs.q: How are leap years handled in reverse?
faqs.a: Automatically. Subtracting 1 year from 29 February 2024 gives 28 February 2023, and subtracting 4 years gives 29 February 2020.

faqs.q: Can I go forward with this tool?
faqs.a: This tool only moves backwards. To go forward in time, use the Add to a Date tool.

faqs.q: What does 'days ago' mean in the results?
faqs.a: How many days the resulting date lies in the past relative to today - handy for 'how long ago was that?' questions.

faqs.q: Is this the same as using a negative number in the Date Calculator?
faqs.a: Effectively yes for days. This dedicated page also supports weeks, months and years with the same one-click simplicity.
